meta.title: Who really said "The most violent element in society is ignorance"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified. Emma Goldman wrote it in her 1910 essay Anarchism: What It Really Stands For — but the famous one-liner is a clause cut from a longer question.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The most violent element in society is ignorance'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Emma Goldman — from Anarchism and Other Essays (1910). But the popular version drops the half that gives it its point.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1869–1940 · Anarchist writer, lecturer & editor of Mother Earth
answer.sourceLine: Goldman wrote the line in “Anarchism: What It Really Stands For,” the lead essay of Anarchism and Other Essays (New York: Mother Earth Publishing Association, 1910). The famous one-liner is genuine but truncated — in the book it is a clause inside a rhetorical question: “How is the ordinary man to know that the most violent element in society is ignorance; that its power of destruction is the very thing Anarchism is combating?”

source.excerpt: The emotions of the ignorant man are continuously kept at a pitch by the most blood-curdling stories about Anarchism. Not a thing too outrageous to be employed against this philosophy and its exponents. … Destruction and violence! How is the ordinary man to know that the most violent element in society is ignorance; that its power of destruction is the very thing Anarchism is combating?
trail: Goldman published the line in her first book, Anarchism and Other Essays ↗, brought out in 1910 by the Mother Earth Publishing Association — the publishing arm of her own journal — and containing the essay “Anarchism: What It Really Stands For.”
The Open Library catalogue record ↗ gives the first edition as New York, Mother Earth Publishing Association, 1910, 277 pages.
Wikisource ↗ and Project Gutenberg ↗ both carry the sentence verbatim in that essay, as does The Anarchist Library ↗, which names its copy text as the second revised edition of 1911.
Page images of the Mother Earth printing are online at the Internet Archive ↗, digitised from the Rutgers University Libraries copy.
source.excerptNote: The line that circulates today is the emphasised clause, lifted out of the question and set down as a standalone maxim.

author.name: Emma Goldman
author.heading: Who was Emma Goldman?
author.metaLine: 1869–1940 · Anarchist writer, lecturer & editor of Mother Earth
author.bio: Born in Kaunas in 1869 in what was then the Russian Empire, Emma Goldman emigrated to the United States in 1885 and became the most notorious anarchist orator in America — and the editor of the journal Mother Earth, whose publishing arm brought out her first book. Anarchism and Other Essays (1910) was that book: essays on prisons, patriotism, political violence, marriage, and the “traffic in women.” She was deported from the United States in 1919 and died in Toronto in 1940.

misattribution.heading: Genuine — but not as it’s usually printed
misattribution.intro: This one survives the usual test: it really is Goldman, and the book is easy to check. What has gone missing is the sentence around it — and, on some sites, any source at all.

items.why: Goodreads ↗ prints the bare sentence with no work, essay or year attached, under a standing notice that its quotes are added by users and are not verified. The original is not a statement but a question: “How is the ordinary man to know that…”

LibQuotes ↗ sources the line to a 2015 Sheba Blake Publishing edition of Anarchism and Other Essays — a modern reissue, not the 1910 Mother Earth Publishing Association original in which the sentence first appeared.

Goldman is a heavy magnet for invented quotations. The most-shared of them — “If voting changed anything, it would be made illegal” — sits in the Disputed section of her Wikiquote page ↗, which finds no evidence she said it and traces the earliest known example to a 1976 opinion piece by Robert S. Borden in The Sun of Lowell, Massachusetts.

misattribution.truthLine: The eight famous words are authentically Goldman’s, and you can read them in context in Chapter 1 on Wikisource ↗ — but quote them with the half that follows, or you lose the argument she was making.

context.heading: Why the missing half matters
lead: Goldman was not writing an aphorism about education. She was answering a smear. The paragraph opens with the press caricature of anarchism — “Destruction and violence!” — and her sentence turns the charge around: the thing actually doing the destroying, she argues, is the ignorance that keeps the public terrified of ideas it has never examined. The line is a rebuttal, not a maxim.

Stripped of that setting, the sentence reads like a genial plea for literacy, which is roughly how it circulates today on posters and quote sites. Restored to the page, it is a working anarchist in 1910 telling readers that the mob frightened of her philosophy is the more dangerous party. Same eight words, a noticeably sharper point.
detailsBody: “Anarchism: What It Really Stands For” is the opening argumentative essay of Anarchism and Other Essays, Goldman’s first book, issued by the publishing arm of her own journal Mother Earth. A second revised edition followed in 1911; the sentence is unchanged in the transcriptions of that 1911 text.

The essay’s method throughout is this same inversion — taking the words used against anarchism (destruction, violence, crime) and reassigning them to the institutions doing the accusing. Elsewhere in the same essay: “Crime is naught but misdirected energy.”
context.pull: In the book it is not a statement at all. It is the middle of a question.

sourcesVerified.claim: The sentence "the most violent element in society is ignorance" appears verbatim in Emma Goldman's essay "Anarchism: What It Really Stands For", within the question "How is the ordinary man to know that the most violent element in society is ignorance; that its power of destruction is the very thing Anarchism is combating?"; the page presents the 1911 second revised edition.

Project Gutenberg EBook #2162 (Anarchism and Other Essays) contains the sentence "the most violent element in society is ignorance; that its power of destruction is the very thing Anarchism is combating" in the essay "Anarchism: What It Really Stands For".
The Anarchist Library's transcription contains the full sentence and states its copy text as the Second Revised Edition, New York-London: Mother Earth Publishing Association, 1911.
The full paragraph, ending in the question containing "the most violent element in society is ignorance", is reproduced from Goldman's 1910 essay "Anarchism".

Anarchism and Other Essays was first published in 1910 by the Mother Earth Publishing Association, runs to 277 pages in the first edition, includes the essay "Anarchism: What It Really Stands For", and contains a biographic sketch by Hippolyte Havel.
Catalogue record: Anarchism and Other Essays, Emma Goldman, Mother Earth Publishing Association, New York, 1910, 277 pages.
The Internet Archive item is a scan of Emma Goldman's Anarchism and Other Essays, Mother Earth Publishing Association, New York, 1911, 277 pages, digitised from the Rutgers University Libraries copy.

Emma Goldman was born 27 June 1869 in Kaunas (then Russian Empire), died 14 May 1940 in Toronto, emigrated to the United States in 1885, was deported in 1919, and was an anarchist revolutionary, political activist and writer.

Goodreads shows the standalone sentence "The most violent element in society is ignorance." attributed to Emma Goldman with no source work or page cited, under a notice that quotes are added by the community and are not verified.
LibQuotes attributes the line to Emma Goldman and cites it to a 2015 Sheba Blake Publishing edition of Anarchism and Other Essays rather than the 1910 original.

Wikiquote's Emma Goldman page lists "If voting changed anything, it would be made illegal" in its Disputed section, stating there is no evidence she said it and giving the earliest known example as Robert S. Borden's 1976 opinion piece in The Sun (Lowell, Massachusetts); the page's sourced sections do not list "the most violent element in society is ignorance".
